Question_Text: Is there an Executive (or executive position) who champions data and analytics or innovation? (This might include a Chief Data Officer, Chief Analytics Officer, or BICC Executive Sponsor or similar titles).
Emerging: Organisation structure siloed to focus on localised efforts
Developing: Organisation structure supports targeted enterprise needs and initiatives
Practicing: Business structure supports most enterprise needs & localised efforts
Innovating: Business organised to deliver and considers operational and broader strategic needs
Leading: Business structure adapts to change whilst providing high quality operations
Roles: Business Sponsor; Program & Project Management; Power User; End User; C-Level
Review_Types: Big Data Capability Review; Data Warehouse Maturity Review; Ecosystem Architecture Review; AI and Machine Learning Review; Custom Review

Question_Text: Do your Executives get the data and analytic results that they need?
Emerging: Access to less than half the analytics outputs that are required.
Developing: Access to some of the analytics outputs though missing key components.  Value prop measured at silo-level, not overall
Practicing: Access to most of the analytics outputs
Innovating: Access to all data required but analytics are mostly retrospective or time-delayed
Leading: Analytics outputs received in real-time and alerts in place on event triggers
Roles: Business Sponsor; C-Level
Review_Types: Big Data Capability Review; Data Warehouse Maturity Review; Ecosystem Architecture Review; AI and Machine Learning Review; Custom Review

Question_Text: How effectively is data and analytics used to support business processes?
Emerging: No analytics are in use.  Decisions are based on gut-feel and historical data
Developing: Analytics are occasionally used to advise on strategic decisions
Practicing: Analytics are available for most decisions and are sometimes used to over-ride gut feel decisions
Innovating: Most strategic and tactical decisions are based on analytic outcomes, and some operational decisions are automated based on analytic models
Leading: Analytics drives operational and strategic value differentiation from the market
Roles: Business Sponsor; Business Analyst; Data Analyst/Modeller/Scientist; Data Engineer; IT Management; Program & Project Management; Power User; End User; C-Level
Review_Types: Big Data Capability Review; Data Warehouse Maturity Review; Ecosystem Architecture Review; AI and Machine Learning Review; Custom Review

Question_Text: Does your organisation have an "Analytics as a Service" function (either internally or contracted externally) where analytics skills (ranging from report developers through to data scientists) are available on call to assist in delivering business outcomes?
Roles: Business Sponsor; Business Analyst; Data Analyst/Modeller/Scientist; Architect; Data Engineer; IT Management; IT Operations; Program & Project Management; Power User; End User; C-Level
Review_Types: Big Data Capability Review; Data Warehouse Maturity Review; Ecosystem Architecture Review; AI and Machine Learning Review; Custom Review

Question_Text: How do senior executives communicate the vision and goals? Are their direct reports and their organizations aware of the enterprise vision and goals?  Are their direct reports and their organizations aware of areas specific vision and goals and how those support the enterprise?
Emerging: There is little or no communication of the analytics vision and goals across the organisation
Developing: Inconsistent but improving company communications about the vision and goals. There are separate analytics visions for each business unit or a single corporate goal that is not communicated
Practicing: Company goals, vision and status are regularly communicated. Executives work towards formulating a shared analytics vision, understanding how each component works together
Innovating: Executives champion and promote the broader vision along with how their area contributes to that vision
Leading: Communications channels are used to effectively update the internal organisation, their customers and the broader industry
Roles: Business Sponsor; IT Management; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: If you have multiple business units, do they share a common vision for data and analytics?
Emerging: There is no enterprise vision and minimal collaboration across departments
Developing: There is no enterprise vision but there is collaboration across departments
Practicing: There is a draft vision in place supported by most executives across most departments
Innovating: There is a shared strategic vision.  Executives champion initiatives
Leading: There is shared strategic and operational vision that leads the industry
Roles: Business Sponsor; Architect; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: Is there a primary driver in your industry that is moving you toward a specific vision or capability?
Roles: Business Sponsor; Business Analyst; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: Are there regulatory/compliance needs driving your organization’s priorities?
Roles: Business Sponsor; Architect; IT Management; IT Operations; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: What are the business’s biggest challenges in getting the information they need from IT?
Roles: Business Sponsor; Business Analyst; Architect; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: What are IT’s biggest challenges in providing the data and the tools needed by the business?
Roles: Business Sponsor; Architect; IT Management; IT Operations
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: What are your strategic business initiatives for the next 12-18 months? What would the Executives say are the most pressing issues or challenges with analytics or data?
Roles: Business Sponsor; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: What needs or questions does your business have that is currently not able to be addressed with your existing analytics and data warehouse environment?
Roles: Business Sponsor; Business Analyst; Data Analyst/Modeller/Scientist; Architect; IT Management; Program & Project Management; Power User; End User; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: Who develops the overall data and analytics strategy?  Is there an analytic roadmap? If so, who is responsible for executing and updating the roadmap?
Emerging: There is no broader business strategy for analytics and data
Developing: A business strategy for analytics and data is emerging with a few key metrics defined
Practicing: A business strategy that has been defined and agreed for data and analytics
Innovating: A business strategy that shows analytics and data as a key part of the overall organisation strategy is in place and most metrics are defined
Leading: The Analytics and Data strategy is a key differentiator and shows how the organisation uses analytics and data now and into the future
Roles: Business Sponsor; Architect; IT Management; Program & Project Management
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: How are executives kept informed of priority projects and their status?
Emerging: There is no project status reporting capability
Developing: Project sponsors are updated monthly on their specific projects
Practicing: A company-wide program office provides weekly or monthly reports on the status of all analytics projects
Innovating: Some projects are delivered with project tracking tools that provide daily status updates and tracking
Leading: A company-wide daily project status dashboard provides overview information with drill-down capabilities showing detailed project status based on project tracking tools
Roles: Business Sponsor; Architect; IT Management; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: How involved are senior executives involved in the review and resolution of cross-functional issues? How are they involved in the prioritization and budgeting of projects? Is there an executive champion assigned to critical projects or programs?
Emerging: There is no executive council or forum responsible for the vision, enterprise program or project execution. There are no standard processes for resolving cross-department conflicts
Developing: An Executive Council or Steering Committee has been formed to direct and oversee a critical project or program. An escalation process for resolution of critical issues is put in place
Practicing: An Executive Steering committee regularly sets direction, resolves escalated program conflicts or issues and communicates updates
Innovating: An Executive Steering Committee oversees direction and steers the analytics program for the company, promoting alignment and innovation
Leading: An Executive Steering Committee sets shared direction and champions projects leading to new insights
Roles: Business Sponsor; IT Management; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: How are data and analytic needs reviewed, prioritized and budgeted?
Emerging: Discovery is not treated separately from projects.  Executives not involved. Failures are covered up.
Developing: Analytics Discovery is funded as phase 1 of planned analytics projects
Practicing: Some discovery projects are funded at business unit level.  Executives embarrassed by failures
Innovating: Programmatic approach to discovery (e.g. A/B testing etc.) appears in some business units.  Executives of those units involved in prioritisation
Leading: Organisation-wide adoption of analytics discovery with executives involved in both successes and failures.  Corporate-wide  prioritisation and funding controls
Roles: Business Sponsor; Business Analyst; Data Analyst/Modeller/Scientist; Architect; IT Management; Program & Project Management
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: Is an approved business case required for analytics projects?
Emerging: Inconsistent project prioritization and funding processes
Developing: High level discussions to prioritize and determine selected project funding
Practicing: Repeatable prioritisation and funding process with high level business cases
Innovating: Prioritization and funding processed work well and provide path for new ideas.  Business case defines and tracks metrics
Leading: Prioritisation and funding promote operational improvements and strategic efforts.  Metrics effectively gathering and analysed to determine business case success
Roles: Business Sponsor; IT Management; Program & Project Management
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: Describe the process for identifying and prioritizing projects.  Describe the criteria used when prioritizing (i.e. Complexity, Costs, Projected Benefits, Prerequisite Needs, Resource Needs, etc.). How far out does the planning go?
Emerging: Inconsistent project prioritization and funding processes
Developing: High level discussions to prioritize and determine selected project funding
Practicing: Repeatable prioritization and funding process exists
Innovating: Prioritization and funding processes work well and provide path for operational improvements and new ideas
Leading: Prioritization and funding promote discovery efforts, operational improvements and the strategic vision
Roles: Business Sponsor; Business Analyst; Architect; IT Management; Program & Project Management
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: Do all projects fall into this process, or are there different processes based on the project’s estimated cost, resource needs, or business function?
Emerging: Little differentiation between how projects supporting operations and the strategic vision are funded or prioritized
Developing: Business Cases are required for strategic or large value projects.
Practicing: All projects require business cases, with the level of detail appropriate for the size of the investment.  Different paths for approval for different project types (discovery, strategic, operational, improvement etc.) may start to appear
Innovating: Differentiated paths exist for discovery, operational and strategic projects.  All project types require some financial justification.  Creative funding ideas encourage continuous improvement.
Leading: Prioritization promotes and funds discovery projects quickly and differently from operational needs.  A consistent path exists for identifying and promoting strategic projects
Roles: Business Sponsor; Business Analyst; Architect; IT Management; Program & Project Management
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: How are potential projects estimated or qualified in preparation for the prioritization or funding process?
Emerging: Estimates are prepared based on gut feel.
Developing: Prior historical outcomes are used to estimate value of new discovery projects
Practicing: Discovery projects are not estimated.  Operational and strategic projects are, based on historical proof points or estimated business value
Innovating: Discovery projects are not estimated.  Operational and strategic projects are, based on reliable financial modelling.
Leading: Discovery projects (e.g. A/B testing) are used to provide qualified estimates for larger projects
Roles: Business Sponsor; Business Analyst; Architect; IT Management; Program & Project Management
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: For those projects that do not qualify for prioritization and funding process, how are resources allocated and tracked? How does the business fund analytic discovery?
Emerging: Annual headcount budget allocated to cover all non-project activities.  No value tracking is done for this time
Developing: Annual headcount budget allocated to cover all non-project activities.  Effort is sometimes tracked and reported against task
Practicing: Annual headcount budget allocated to cover all non-project activities.  Effort is consistently tracked and reported against task assigned
Innovating: Investment pool is allocated to fund small analytics activities. Business value statements are submitted and reported for all non-project activities.  Resources are assigned to highest business value first
Leading: Central pool of investment funds and resources exists for small project activity.  Resoucres are allocated based on business value which is tracked and reported on
Roles: Business Sponsor; IT Management; Program & Project Management
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: What is your baseline for projecting data and analytic funding and resource demand? Do you start out with an annual budget that is driven by last year's budget (or example, plus or minus 5%)?  What is included in the funding of data and analytic initiatives (i.e. architecture, technology, business and IT resources, contractors, etc.)?
Emerging: Annual headcount budget allocated to cover all non-project activities.  No value tracking is done for this time
Developing: Annual headcount budget allocated to cover all non-project activities.  Effort is sometimes tracked and reported against task
Practicing: Annual headcount budget allocated to cover all non-project activities.  Effort is consistently tracked and reported against task assigned
Innovating: Investment pool is allocated to fund small analytics activities. Business value statements are submitted and reported for all non-project activities.  Resources are assigned to highest business value first
Leading: Central pool of investment funds and resources exists for small project activity.  Resources are allocated based on business value which is tracked and reported on
Roles: Business Sponsor; IT Management; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: Who is the final decision maker for funding and prioritization?   Is there an executive level position that provides input for data and analytic needs and priorities to the final decision maker?
Emerging: For larger projects, decisions to fund or proceed are made by a single sponsor
Developing: Different business areas are starting to collaborate and partner when funding initiatives
Practicing: A standard prioritization process, shared by business and IT, exists.   Thresholds determine when a project or system request requires formal funding and prioritisation
Innovating: Prioritization and funding processes work well and provide path for operational improvements and new ideas.  Thresholds effectively promote discovert and completion of smaller projects whilst requiring estimating and design for projects with cross-organisational impacts
Leading: Prioritization promotes and funds discovery projects quickly and differently from operational needs.  A consistent path exists for identifying and promoting strategic projects
Roles: Business Sponsor; IT Management; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: Where in your organisation do Data Scientists sit?  Are they in departmental / line of business roles, or in IT, or in a central organisational structure?
Emerging: There are no Data Scientists
Developing: Data Scientists are in IT
Practicing: Data Scientists are in line of business roles and no co-operation exists between groups
Innovating: Data Scientists are in line of business groups but there is formal co-ordination and co-operation between groups
Leading: Central pool of Data Scientists and some resources exists for small project activity.  Resources are allocated based on business value which is tracked and reported on
Roles: Business Sponsor; Data Analyst/Modeller/Scientist; IT Management; Program & Project Management
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: IIs there a pool of IT or analytic development resources shared across the business units? Are there different IT or analytic teams for applications and support?  (For example, are dataa & analytic teams organized to support specific tools or enterprise applications, like SAP?).  What about other cross functional teams, such as a BICC or a Data Management or Data Governance team?
Emerging: Annual headcount budget allocated to cover all IT activities.  No value tracking is done for this time
Developing: Annual headcount budget allocated to support.  Effort is sometimes tracked and reported against task
Practicing: Annual headcount budget allocated to cover all IT activities.  Effort is consistently tracked and reported against task assigned
Innovating: Investment pool is allocated to fund design and architecture of new projects. Business value statements are submitted and reported for all activities.  Resoures are assigned to highest business value first
Leading: Central pool of investment funds and resources exists for small project activity.  Resoures are allocated based on business value which is tracked and reported on
Roles: Business Sponsor; IT Management; Program & Project Management
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: How are corporate projects charged back to the business units?  Do you have charge-back mechanism for CPU usage, I/O, or data storage?
Emerging: No Charge-back is done
Developing: Charge-back is done based on overall system operational cost, split by the number of departments using the system
Practicing: Charge-back is done based on a basic IT metric such as CPU, # of users, or Storage space
Innovating: Charge-back partially done on the basis of all IT resources consumed, with separate metrics driving different cost bases
Leading: Charge-back consistently done on the basis of all IT resources consumed, with separate metrics driving different cost bases
Roles: Business Sponsor; IT Management; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: Are business cases required to allocate funded?  Are business cases initiated by the business or IT?  What criteria are required for a business case to be approved?
Emerging: Estimates are prepared based on gut feel and generated by either business or IT.  No formal standards required.  No central lodgement and tracking
Developing: Business Cases are standardised in requirements, but approved at business unit level inconsistently and neither centrally lodged nor tracked
Practicing: Business Case submission and approval processes are standardised but slow.  Tracking is partial or incomplete.
Innovating: Business Case submission and approval process is supported by process automation and can be done rapidly if required.
Leading: Business Case submission and approval process is supported by process automation and can be done rapidly if required.
Roles: Business Sponsor; IT Management; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: How do you know when it is time to change your solutions or divest of the solutions you have? How do you balance investing and divesting? How is this planned for in your budget?
Emerging: No end-of-life planning is done
Developing: Funds are requested based on a case-by-case basis when assets fail or emergency replacements are required
Practicing: Systems with known end-of-life issues are planned to be replaced in the annual budget
Innovating: A systems review is conducted annually to determine which systems need replacement, based on a fixed pool of allocated funds
Leading: A portfolio approach is used with funding assigned to cover discovery, deployment, improvements, operations and asset retirement
Roles: Business Sponsor; IT Management; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: Who has the CAPEX and resource budget for IT? Who is the decision maker on data and analytic investment?
Emerging: Analytics are funded from resource headcount rather than as projects.  IT owns the CAPEX and IT resource budget
Developing: Analytics are funded by business sources.  IT owns the CAPEX and IT resource budget
Practicing: Analytics are funded from business sources.  IT owns a portion of the CAPEX budget for infrastructure but business can fund new IT capability as part of business cases
Innovating: Funds are distributed based on common agreement amongst business and IT executives on an annual basis.  Project funding is approved by business case
Leading: Discovery analytics are separately funded.  General investment in split between IT for infrastructure and operations, and business for development of new capability
Roles: Business Sponsor; IT Management; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: Are analytics, IT, or business oriented projects separately or independently funded?
Emerging: All projects funded using the same ad hoc process
Developing: All projects funded using the same structured process
Practicing: Business and IT-driven projects are funded from separate sources.
Innovating: Some or most IT projects are linked and funded together with a relevant business project that requires the capability
Leading: Discovery projects are funded separately, whilst Business and IT projects are funded based on business strategy alignment
Roles: Business Sponsor; IT Management; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: Do you have a long term roadmap that you follow that incorporates the major initiatives over the next few years?  If so, how is that managed?
Emerging: There is no long term roadmap. Individual projects are approved independently and without strategic planning
Developing: Major operational systems have long term roadmaps but analytics systems are not covered
Practicing: Business and IT stakeholders come together to develop and approve a strategic program over at least 1 year timelines, including analytics systems
Innovating: Program Management effectively co-ordinates the execution of projects within a strategic roadmap covering operational and analytics systems
Leading: Program management manages to a strategic vision but delivers in adaptable and agile ways to changing business needs
Roles: Business Sponsor; IT Management; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: How are the milestones between different projects and initiatives coordinated?
Emerging: Managing across projects or initiatives is difficult.  Projects often having competing needs and overlapping objectives
Developing: A process of managing across projects has been defined for critical programs
Practicing: Program management standards and processes are leveraged to drive alignment and more effectively leverage resources across projects
Innovating: Proactive program management is done to keep related projects aligned and alert the team of other issues or changes that may impact program delivery
Leading: The Program Management function is seen as best in the industry, regularly contributing to efficient business change
Roles: Business Sponsor; IT Management; Program & Project Management
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: How does the organisation track value delivered from project investments?
Emerging: No tracking is performed.
Developing: Some larger projects are assessed for success, but little attention is paid from lessons learned.
Practicing: Projects are regularly assessed for success and these lessons are incorporated into corporate memory and process improvements
Innovating: Smaller projects are performed faster and more regularly, providing early feedback onto project success and allowing failing projects to be terminated quickly
Leading: Large initiatives are delivered in small chunks to allow for faster failure.  Smaller discovery initiatives are implemented to predict future value.
Roles: Business Sponsor; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: How are the ROI numbers in a business justification (e.g. Business Case)  estimated and vetted?
Emerging: No ROI numbers are required
Developing: ROI numbers are estimated.  Larger projects are sometimes subjected to financial review of the ROI numbers by an independent team.
Practicing: ROI numbers are estimated for all projects.  A consistent set of parameters and values is used in all business cases. ROI numbers for larger projects are required to be independently vetted (e.g. by Finance or similar). s
Innovating: A consistent set of parameters and values (and sometimes a standard financial model) is used.  The estimated cost savings or revenue improvements are required to be adjusted in the sponsor's budget for the following year if the project is approved.
Leading: A consistent financial model for project ROI is used.  The financial model is improved on a regular basis to better predict outcomes.  Discovery projects are approved separately for blue-sky analytics concepts.
Roles: Business Sponsor; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: How does the organization monitor and measure the effectiveness (business value) of data and analytics to a business process?
Roles: Business Sponsor; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: Does each business case contain a measurement plan, which includes determining baseline metrics against which improvements can be projected (and presumably measured)?  How do you know if or when business case projections are achieved?  Is this something that is regularly measured after a project is implemented?
Emerging: No tracking of results is done
Developing: Some projects contain measurement plans and are assessed by the Project Manager approx. 3-6 months after completion
Practicing: A corporate mandate for measurement plans and tracking results of business cases exists but it is incompletely complied with
Innovating: Measurement plans exist and tracking the results of business cases is done once at a specified point after project completion
Leading: Measurement plans exist and tracking the results of business cases is automated and continuously updated.  Deployment methods allow for easy tracking of change
Roles: Business Sponsor; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: Describe the process of tracking and reporting on actual results. Are baseline metrics established consistent with the business case? Does the ROI analysis include projections of investment costs? Does the ROI analysis include projections of ongoing operating costs such as additional IT maintenance feed, new headcount, etc.?
Emerging: No tracking of results is done
Developing: The project manager is responsible for results evaluation which is performed manually
Practicing: A central team (either corporately or per business unit) records the approved ROI metrics and collects data from the project manager to assess success
Innovating: A central team (either corporately or per business unit) records the approved ROI metrics and performs a monthly assessment of success to issue a report
Leading: A central team (either corporately or per business unit) enters the approved ROI metrics into an automated system that tracks project outcomes daily
Roles: Business Sponsor; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: Do projects consider business and IT costs, needs and priorities?  Which ones get higher exposure/priority?
Emerging: Business value is the only focus.  Costs are considered, but constraints are not.
Developing: Larger projects get executive attention but still do not consider constraints or non-financial measures
Practicing: Business and IT costs are included, and some sense of resource constraints is sometimes included.  Senior executives approve all medium to large projects
Innovating: Resource and capacity constraints become commonly included in decision making.  Senior executives set thresholds and capacities, which are then applied by mid management for smaller projects
Leading: Prioritisation in a scarce environment becomes the key driver for project prioritization.  Business and IT constraints include ability to train staff in new procedures, change management capacity and other factors are regularly considered
Roles: Business Sponsor; IT Management; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: Are business cases for IT or other operational investments required?
Emerging: No business cases are required for IT or operational investments
Developing: Infrastructure investments are assessed in the same process as business-initiated changes
Practicing: Infrastructure investments are assessed separately to business-initiated change, within an assigned funding pool
Innovating: Business Cases for Infrastructure investments are required but assessed separately to business-initiated change
Leading: A portfolio approach is used to balance funding across infrastructure, projects and discovery activities to enable all types of projects to progress.
Roles: Business Sponsor; IT Management; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: Who is accountable for achievement of ROI goals? What corrective actions are taken if results fall short of projected goals?  Who is responsible for initiating and implementing the corrective actions?
Emerging: No tracking of results is done
Developing: The project manager is responsible for the achievement of the ROI Goals.  No corrective actions are taken if the ROI is not delivered
Practicing: The project sponsor is responsible for the achievement of the ROI goals.  A review is conducted if the ROI goals are not met.  Corrective actions are assigned to the Project Sponsor by the steering committee to resolve the issues
Innovating: The project sponsor is responsible for the achievement of ROI, and a standards Post Implementation Review is conducted to learn for future projects.
Leading: ROI achievement is consistently measured and used to assess management effectiveness
Roles: Business Sponsor; IT Management; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: Are metrics common across projects, or specific to a single project? How are users educated about ROI, the metrics, and the process?
Roles: Business Sponsor; IT Management; Program & Project Management
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: When and how is the business case process initiated?  What does the business case consider?
Roles: Business Sponsor; IT Management; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review

Question_Text: Do the business users have access to the data they need to complete their reporting and analysis?
Emerging: Some required data not available for review or analysis
Developing: Data available for operational needs but only through transactional systems
Practicing: Business has access to all operational data needed and some data for exploration or discovery
Innovating: Data coverage includes all business functions and needs
Leading: Analytics dta avilable for all business functions and related needs
Roles: Business Sponsor; Business Analyst; Data Analyst/Modeller/Scientist; Program & Project Management; Power User; End User
Review_Types: Big Data Capability Review; Data Warehouse Maturity Review; Ecosystem Architecture Review; AI and Machine Learning Review

Question_Text: Have you considered the impact of “big data” on your data integration; e.g., are you able to link social media data to your Customer or Product master?
Emerging: No "big data" is captured
Developing: Big Data is maintained separately from operational data and cannot be integrated
Practicing: Ad hoc integration using approximation techniques are in place on an as-needs basis
Innovating: Specific matching keys (e.g. credit card or customer name) allow for moderate levels of matching
Leading: Specific programs are in place (e.g. self registration, cookies, customer details matching) to increase the ability to link between Big Data sources and operational master data
Roles: Business Sponsor; Data Analyst/Modeller/Scientist; Architect; IT Management
Review_Types: Big Data Capability Review; Data Warehouse Maturity Review; Ecosystem Architecture Review; AI and Machine Learning Review

Question_Text: How effective are the security and privacy management policies and processes of your organisation?
Emerging: Security and Privacy polies are outdated or insufficient
Developing: Security and privacy needs and regulartory requirements are understood and appropriate management is being initiated
Practicing: Security and privacy policies have been implemented to meet the security and regulatory requirements of the enterprise
Innovating: A comprehensive security management process is in place for the enterprise. Security and Privacy policies are solid, allowing easy access to those authorised, but preventing access to others
Leading: There is a continuous process improvement approach to security management with an understanding that data sources and types are continuously evolving
Roles: Business Sponsor; IT Management; Program & Project Management
Review_Types: Big Data Capability Review; Data Warehouse Maturity Review; Ecosystem Architecture Review; AI and Machine Learning Review

Question_Text: How often is data updated?  Are there certain data only available or updated daily or weekly?
Emerging: Data for analysis is updated on a daily basis and may be out of date when analysed
Developing: Data is kept current ofr targetted business needs though some challenges remain
Practicing: Data currency is acceptable
Innovating: Data is current for discovery and production purposes
Leading: Data is up to date with future predicted data effecively leveraged
Roles: Data Analyst/Modeller/Scientist; Architect; IT Management
Review_Types: Big Data Capability Review; Data Warehouse Maturity Review; Ecosystem Architecture Review; AI and Machine Learning Review

Question_Text: Is the data in the analytics ecosystem of sufficient quality to meet most business analytics needs?
Emerging: Data Quality is not measured and is known to be poor
Developing: There are some data quality processes in place - usually manual and without data profiling
Practicing: Data quality is acceptable, with data stewardship programs in place
Innovating: Data quality is maintained and managed to standards and metrics
Leading: Data quality is effectively managed with meaningful metrics for accountability
Roles: Business Sponsor; Business Analyst; Data Analyst/Modeller/Scientist; Architect; IT Management; Program & Project Management; Power User; End User
Review_Types: Big Data Capability Review; Data Warehouse Maturity Review; Ecosystem Architecture Review; AI and Machine Learning Review

Question_Text: How much historical data is immediately available (not archived) for online analysis?  Does the amount of online historical data support analysis requirements such as seasonal, current versus prior period, and period + 1 (13, 25, or 37 month) for trend identification?
Emerging: Historical data is difficult to access
Developing: Some historical data is available
Practicing: Defined processes exist for sourcing and access to current and historical data
Innovating: Historical data is available for 1-2 years and archived (and recoverable) beyond that.  Sometimes summary historical data is always available.
Leading: Historical data is available for long periods of time but on slower response, lower cost platforms
Roles: IT Management
Review_Types: Big Data Capability Review; Data Warehouse Maturity Review; Ecosystem Architecture Review; AI and Machine Learning Review

Question_Text: Does your organisation have a defined information or data strategy.  Is that strategy capable of dealing with big data as well as traditional data sources?
Roles: Business Sponsor; Business Analyst; Data Analyst/Modeller/Scientist; IT Management

Question_Text: Does the business know which systems and tools to use to achieve the desired business analytics outcome? Are all desired business analytics outcomes supported by some form of technology?

Leading: An analytic ecosystem encompassing a wide variety of storage and processing architectures is in place and effectively meeting needs

Review_Types: Big Data Capability Review; Data Warehouse Maturity Review; Ecosystem Architecture Review; AI and Machine Learning Review

Question_Text: Do you have a Technology Strategy defined that supports the provisioning of technology to deliver the desired business analytics outcomes? Does this strategy address short term and long term business analytics outcomes?

Developing: Technology functions are defined in independent silos to enable more effective support for a targeted set of business functions or analytic needs. For example, defined for a data mart or data exploration zone.
Practicing: Technology capabilities are defined for major business functions and business analytics outcomes. This enables consistency and standardisation across the provisioning of technology.
Innovating: The Technology Strategy guides outcomes to meet current and future business goals.
Leading: The Technology Strategy rapidly evolves and guides outcomes to meet current and future business goals.
Roles: Architect; IT Management; Program & Project Management; C-Level

Question_Text: Systems Section - Roadmap

Emerging: There is no roadmap in place to shown when or if technology capabilities will be provisioned to support business analytics outcomes.
Developing: I.T. is developing a near to mid-term technology roadmap to give the business visibility of when analytic capabilities will become available.
Practicing: A near to mid-term roadmap guides the provisioning of analytic capabilities and is used by the business to align business analytics outcomes with analytic capabilities.
Innovating: The roadmap extends to the long term and  allows the business to be ready for future capabilities as they are needed.
Leading: The roadmap rapidly evolves and guides outcomes giving the business extensive responsiveness to the changing business landscape.
Roles: Business Sponsor; Architect; IT Management; Program & Project Management; C-Level
Review_Types: Data Warehouse Maturity Review; Ecosystem Architecture Review

Question_Text: When evaluating new business solutions, are there recommended system standards for the platforms, operating systems, data bases, file systems, open source usage, cloud, etc.?  How do these standards impact the decision to move forward with a new business solution?

Developing: Policies are introduced to provide consistency and standardisation. I.T. is introducing governance over Systems Architecture.
Practicing: Policies and standards provide consistency of support and capability across business analytics outcomes. Duplication of I.T. functions outside of I.T. is minimised.
Innovating: A formal Systems Architecture approach and governance provides a framework for business to easily move forward with a new business solution based on policies and standards as well as test out new/emerging capabilities.
Leading: An evolving Systems Architecture enables and supports current business needs whilst allowing the business to adapt to new concepts and changing business needs.

Question_Text: A single view of customer across the organisation?
Emerging: No clean source of integrated customer information. View of the customer is not well defined and is inconsistent across business units. Many definitions of organisation and associated subject areas such as channel. Interactions are not captured across all channels.
Developing: One company wide definition of customer widely accepted, but still with some non-associated functions having differing definitions. All transactions are identified by customer id. Batch updates of changes leads to data latency in the single customer view.
Practicing: One company wide definition of customer and organisation. Customer is identified and addressed the same across the company. Interactions are captured for both known (identified) customers and unknown  (cookie or device ID). Includes additional data such as demographics. Customers are identified individually and by household. Batch updates of changes leads to data latency in the single customer view.
Innovating: One company wide definition of customer and organisation. Customer is identified and addressed the same across the company. A significant percentage of customers can be identified by recent transaction, interactions and segment and treated consistently across channels. Near real time updating of customer identity following changes to core customer data
Leading: One definition of a customer (and its associated hierarchies) across the enterprise, regardless of functional application. A large percentage of customers are identified and the channel experience is coordinated across all channels. Able to determine the customers value and depth of relationship across the company and by business unit.  Interactions of unknown customer is captured and leveraged for personalization. Ability to resolve known and unknown customers and merge customer records using a variety of core customer data attributes and matching techniques.
Roles: Business Sponsor

Question_Text: A Multi-dimensional customer view (360 degree view of customer interactions across all channels and connections)?
Emerging: Basic core feeds of product and transactional data  on weekly basis. Summary online channel data available for both authenticated and non-authenticated sites also loaded on a weekly basis. Detailed click stream not collected or loaded. Interaction data, such as marketing, often stored separately. All data loaded by traditional batch methods
Developing: Core feeds of product and transactional data on a daily basis. Daily loading of click stream data from core sites including tagging and ability to identify user sessions. Data is aggregated to allow summary and dashboard reporting. Interaction data continues to be stored separately
Practicing: Some transactional and product data feeds move to intra-day. Click stream data from core sites is loaded at the detail level daily. Advanced analytics are leveraged to calculate and store derived attributes such as customer revenue and propensity to purchase products. Begin to identify key events and interactions to be integrated into the multi-dimensional view.
Innovating: Detail level clickstream data is loaded intraday. Event table is defined and automated feeds of some types of interactions and events are loaded daily.  Capture and load limited text data sources such as call center transcripts and customer emails and surveys. Additional derived customer attributes such as lifetime value and satisfactions are added.
Leading: Full transactional data is loaded. Detailed clickstream data is loaded in near real time. A wide variety of events and interactions are captured and made available for analytics. Additional text sources such as social media, click to chat and reviews are loaded.
Roles: Business Sponsor
Industries: Retail; Financial; Communications; Manufacturing; Travel & Transport; Energy & Natural Resources; Healthcare
Review_Types: Big Data Capability Review; Data Warehouse Maturity Review; AI and Machine Learning Review; Custom Review

Question_Text: A solid understanding of customer value and profitability?
Emerging:
Customer Profitability capabilities just starting to emerge:
Activity-based costing not available, so value is product focused– e.g., total sales, balances, # products
Calculations based on “averages” used to manage at the customer and product portfolio levels
Developing: Activity-based Profitability results are used to make decisions across products and customer segments, but not yet on individual customers or activities.
Practicing: Organization develops sophistication around sunk profits vs. at-risk profits, when to fully-allocated costs and when to use marginally-allocated costs, etc.  Lifetime Value (LTV) begins to be part of decision processes, though not yet at an advanced level.
Innovating: Profitability results are also used operationally to deliver information and guidance to staff on customer retention, customer experience, pricing and other operational decisions (e.g. fee refunds)
Leading:
Profitability results are used extensively across the organisation to support a wide range of strategic, tactical and operational decision-making, including all of the below, plus:
Performance management and Staff incentivisation
Channel management / channel migration strategy
Use of advanced analytics techniques (e.g.  Clustering, behavioural analysis / path to increased profit)
Roles: Business Sponsor
Industries: Retail; Financial; Communications; Manufacturing; Travel & Transport; Energy & Natural Resources; Healthcare
Review_Types: Big Data Capability Review; Data Warehouse Maturity Review; AI and Machine Learning Review; Custom Review

Question_Text: A Customer Satisfaction Index to measure and manage the impact of interactions on customer satisfaction and experience?

Practicing: Experiment  with  text analytic capabilities (may be outsourced) to understand customer comments on products, service and experience. Limited ability to react to negative comments. Call center is key to identifying customer issues. Advanced analytics deployed to identify limited set of key interactions
Innovating: Build robust cross channel interactions, and touch points. Analyze customer s across touch points to identify interactions that drive positive  or negative  outcomes.
Leading: Incorporate sentiment analysis, multi genre analytics in combination with business rules to calculate customer satisfaction. Scores are operationalized and drive actions to improve processes and customer experience. Active monitoring and alerting on increases and decreases of scores.   CSI becomes integrated with Customer Profitability/Value Management

Question_Text: A Customer Experience Analytic that measures and predicts customer's perceptions of a service or product?

Both internal data and voice of the customer data including external social media data are used to assess customer experience

Question_Text: Contextual Decisioning, that make interactions more relevant by considering other events over space and time as context of the customer interaction
Emerging: Leads/customer segments and offers  generated in batch and presented to channels without regard for context of customer interaction. Manual decisioning used in some channels to select from multiple offers that fits best with interaction reason.
Developing: Some channel systems able to identify high level process being undertaken for customer and pass this information to decision environment at point of interaction. Context drives simple weighted prioritisation of batch pre-generated offers.
Practicing: Context identified, classified and passed all from inbound channels including face to face and digital channels. Allows context of interaction to be included in arbitration / prioritisation rules.
Innovating: Micro context identified in channel such as location, transaction detail, step of process, status of request or browsing history driving improved relevance of offers.
Leading: Automated real-time interactions driven by context input from complex events involving location, transaction detail, step of process, status of request or browsing history plus automated response adaptation driving more refined decisioning and improved relevance of offers.

Question_Text: Call/Contact Center Optimization, increasing the first call resolution and reduce customers returning calls on same topic
Emerging: Provide call centre agent relevant customer data including access to customer events, products purchased , channel interaction updated weekly.  Provide recommedned action or product by customer segment via models updated weekly

Leading: Real –time decisioning presents best message/offer based on context of current and/or  last customer interaction. Create prediction models for when a customer or situation will lead to increased likelihood to complain. Provide call center agents with  prioritized list of remediation. Actions.

Question_Text: Search Engine Optimization, to improve relevancy of web site search results to drive higher conversion

Leading: Automated process to predict and update key words. Ranking algorithms are optimized for best results. Performance of search queries is monitored on a regular basis and declining performance is identified. A/B testing is utilized to measure search query and conversion improvement.

Question_Text: Personalization of offers to move from mass customisation of offers (based on broad segments) to a 1:1 personalisation of customer communications using individual customer data
Emerging: Limited personalisation of basic fields (eg, name). Campaign activity still cell based with no offer customisation capabilities.

Copy and content within an execution can be personalised with individual illustrations. Campaigns can have 000’s of variants.

Multiple assets within a creative can be personalised using document composition technology. Campaigns have millions of unique variants

Question_Text: Next Best Action Arbitration, determing the next best action for a customer when they interact with the company

Developing: Next best action arbitration extended to cover broader set of customer actions driven primarily from individual level decisioning performed against  predictive models.

Innovating: Next best action arbitration for a broad range of customer treatments across a wide range of inbound channels. NBA logic uses diverse sources of data such as customer segmentation, predictive models, triggers and customer value measures.

Question_Text: Product Recommendation, presenting the most relevant product recommendation(s) based upon a customer/prospects interaction and previous behaviour
Emerging: Simple (often binary) product recommendation based upon average customer behaviour (typically at gross product level)
Developing: More complex recommendations based upon segment based customer behaviours
Practicing: Move to individual customer-level recommendations with increasing scope and time horizons – eg product purchase patterns over time  and overlaid with external factors (weather)
Innovating: More extended affinity considerations/models potentially with more diverse offers (eg link or bridge products, directional affinities). Extending the recommendation outside of product only to wider offers – eg based upon past interactions (dropped basket due to excess delivery charges – offer – free delivery). Utilise predictive techniques on attributes driving customer behaviour.
Leading: Highly contextual product offers based upon personal past purchase/browsing histories over extended timescales, fully automated real time delivery, utilising  the fullest extent of external data  (eg. location/weather ) and internal data (store range and stock) and profit optimisation strategies

Question_Text: Multi-Step Campaigns, to create relevant 2-way dialogue with customers by determining next interaction based on outcome of previous interactions
Emerging: Majority of campaigns are single step – monologue based repeated on regular basis
Developing: Use of multi-step starting to be used in some campaigns – primarily to trigger follow up activity to non responders
Practicing: Multi-step approach largely embedded into campaign design. Stepping criteria  uses a small selection of events and triggers such as  customer response outcomes  or non-response
Innovating: Multi-step approach embedded into campaign design. Stepping criteria  uses a variety of events and triggers such as customer response outcomes  and inferred responses. Subsequent steps always re-qualify initial eligibility criteria.
Leading: Advanced use of multi-step techniques to orchestrate customer journeys across channels and create dialogue based approaches. Stepping criteria  uses a variety of events, triggers and customer listening techniques such as response outcomes and inferred responses. Subsequent steps always re-qualify initial product / offer and channel eligibility criteria. Real-time event may over-ride or change  timing or content of next action.

Question_Text: Campaign Effectiveness, analyzing the impact a specific campaign or groups of campaigns against the goal for the campaign and utilise that information to improve the results of future campaigns
Emerging: Basic ability to measure and report upon sales, upgrades, channel usage by the target audience based on actual response or simple inference.
Developing: Commitment to and ability to execute and understand Champion/Challenger (A/B) testing
Practicing: Processes and skills  in place to collect and understand  results by customer segment and micro-segment. Increasing sophistication of inference based measurement accounting for customer variability in following specified calls to action.

Leading: Ability to project the Lifetime Value impact of campaigns based on how the customer responses affect current profitability, loyalty, etc. – and to modify targeting, messaging and offers accordingly to maximize that LTV. Move towards the development of sophisticated marketing attribution techniques to weight campaign contribution versus ATL or other BTL activity over an extended timescale.

Question_Text: Marketing Attribution, to analyse the customer path to conversion to determine the impact of interactions on conversion and attribute the value of each interaction to sales or some other specific conversion type
Emerging: Basic marketing measurement typically a ‘last-click’ type approach. Traditional attribution process runs at a campaign by campaign basis within channels silos. Activity measured limited to sales outcomes. Performed on an ad-hoc basis driven by campaign activity.
Developing: Primarily basic marketing measurement approaches run on a campaign by campaign basis. Campaign measurement process is automated and standard reports are produced. Experimentation started to investigate cross channel attribution methods but no systemised methodology or automated process developed.
Practicing: Marketing attribution process semi automated and runs on a monthly basis. Scope limited to sales based outcomes from highest volume channels. Static reports produced issued to users.
Innovating: Marketing attribution process fully automated and runs on a weekly basis. Scope includes most activity (>80%) including non sales outcomes and model considers interactions from most channels. Regular reporting issued to end users with simple dashboard summary.
Leading: Marketing attribution process fully automated and runs on a daily basis. Scope includes all activity and model considers interactions from all channels. Rich set of dashboards and interactive reporting makes data easily available to end users via self serve tools.
Roles: Business Sponsor

Question_Text: Brand Analytics, to quantify the impact of a company’s brand on marketing and company performance
Emerging: Simple reporting of brand metrics – largely conducted by 3rd party agencies. Little analysis to link specific activity with business outcomes.

Analytics used to drive a growing number of activities such as calendar planning, product development, pricing and media buying.
Leading: Comprehensive range of brand effectiveness metrics – integrating internal and external measures to report on effectiveness of brand building activities – with ability to isolate the impact of specific activities. Analytics used to drive a large number of activities such as calendar planning, product development and media buying. Sophisticated forecasting and simulation models enables optimisation of the media mix and marketing budget. Measures of Brand Equity calculated, tracked and reported,

Question_Text: Research New Product Development Opportunities, to leverage external market research, trends and internal product usage data to support product and packaging design and specifications
Emerging: Little to no investment in researching new product ideas. Decisions made based on past experience and/or personal preferences. Generally repeat what worked last year and plan inventory based on last year’s product usage and sales statistics plus expected growth. Performance depends on the capabilities of individuals or teams and varies with their innate skills, knowledge, and motivations.
Developing: Understanding of the need to efficiently manage the product development lifecycle and the limitation of being reactive to declining product revenue. Utilize surveys and focus groups to understand market direction and identify product categories. Most new product introductions are limited to evolutionary changes.

This process can be characterized as including inputs, standards and procedures for performing the work, metrics for verification, and other standard outputs. Emerging use of analytic techniques, such as sentiment analysis, to better understand customer needs and expectations with the use of customer and usage data
Innovating: Established metrics for product development processes. The development process is predictable because the process is measured and operates within measurable limits. Utilize analytic techniques, such as sentiment analysis, to better understand customer needs and expectations systematically using customer and usage data
Leading: The entire organization is focused on continuous process improvement characterized by an agile new product development methodology. Able to predict emerging trends and gain first mover advantage. Advanced predictive analytics incorporated into methodology.
Roles: Business Sponsor

Review_Types: Big Data Capability Review; Data Warehouse Maturity Review; AI and Machine Learning Review; Custom Review

Question_Text: Predict Business Impact (Discovery), which is the prediction of product launce impact on resources, assets and market adoption, to support business case and investment justification

Question_Text: Source Products and Develop Contracts, including managing costs, risks, quality, service levels and performance of vendors that supply products or raw materials
Emerging: Manual sharing and analysis of demand data and forecasts via spread sheets. Vendor purchasing data includes limited historical data available.  Raw materials data is siloed or non-existent.  Product costs are not known; estimates are used to calculate final (LLC) costs.

Question_Text: Plan Product Investments to Support Go-to-Market Strategy, including holistic evaluation and determination of appropriate initial resource, capital and infrastructural investment for product launch
Emerging: Basic forecasting and allocation practices. No enterprise view of inventory ownership. Go-to-market processes and cycle for each functional unit is lengthy, manual and non-aligned. Siloed processes in place but no cross-function or business cooperation. Promotional inventory based on historical trends. Little variability in assortments
Developing: Improved cross-functional communications during planning process. Basic alignment of some functions and channels. Leverage predictive forecasting practices/ tools  for basic items. New product forecast done via manual historical tracking of similar products/ services. Actual versus Plan reporting to manage performance and adjust future plans. Financial plans and drivers are reconciled to ensure direction and strategy.
Practicing: Cross-function flows still manual but using electronic means. Close alignment among channels and functions, with high level cross-functional cooperation, but on a project-by-project basis. Enterprise inventory visibility enabled. Seasonal forecasting practiced. Automated adjustment of product and location service levels based on product lifecycle stage. Assign products to branch clusters using profile-based attributes such as demographics/ lifestyle, financial profile and perception. Product/ service continuum planning to enable improved take-up rates. Competitor product suite  and pricing tracked. Leverage elasticity models for product campaign and promo inventory management
Innovating: Automation of cross-function approvals. Extensive cooperation, with integration between most functions. SLAs in place for fulfillment and delivery. average demand forecasting practices and tools for multiple product/ service suite. “Buy from anywhere, fulfill from  anywhere” capability enabled.  Automated fulfillment  via  parameters and rules. Full automation of new product introduction and history. Product suite optimized for key customer segments. Rationalization of vendors and product suite based on margin and profitability. analyze product/service continuum gaps. Integrate campaign planning, marketing and inventory planning. Robust calculation of campaign ROI
Leading: Full automation of all workflow driven processes from campaign design to final approvals. Full organizational alignment and integration across channels, functions and business units. Detailed SLAs for fulfillment coupled with transformed culture of collaboration. End to end product management and complete supply chain visibility. “What if” analytics well entrenched.  Unified pricing, campaign and Product suite modeling. Consider near real time competitor product proposition and pricing analytics. Incorporate customer segment definitions into assortment (range) planning process to support customer-centric merchandising across all channels. Track performance of product campaigns in near real time

Question_Text: Adjust Product Lifecycle Pricing, which is the ability to model and proactively set/adjust prices to maximize profit during all life stages of a product
Emerging: Prices points are determined based on established markdown cadence and rules by channel.  Price points set based on rules within operational system or basic buyer formulae.  No formal pricing analytics or pricing organization. Incorporate wallet, discount and loyalty redemption into pricing.

Begin to operationalize seasonal variability of pricing by location and explore elasticity of demand for promotional events. Zone and store level pricing is possible.
Innovating: Experienced pricing team exist that are capable of building new models. Customer data  is incorporated into pricing decisions.  Pricing recommendations are understood and accepted by business users.  Buy Plans and Sales Forecasts are regularly evaluated via scenario planning.  Exploration of channel-driven pricing
Leading: Companies can set price at location or channel level.  Capable of managing dynamic prices in near real time.   Personalized prices based on individual customers is possible, incorporating wallet, discount and loyalty redemption into pricing.   Predictive analytics are consistently used to anticipate performance and to  plan advantageous buys.

Review_Types: Big Data Capability Review; Data Warehouse Maturity Review; AI and Machine Learning Review; Custom Review

Question_Text: Manage Dynamic Pricing, reactively adjusting prices based on resource availabilty to shape demand and manage yeild in right/near-real time.  Prices may fluctuate based on time of day, space and usage amongst other events
Emerging: Pricing scheme update monthly /weekly based on stock  and sales target information (internal information)

Seasonality, order lead time, Time of day
Location of customer/ POS
available stock, strategic product categorization, end-of-life, bridge products  etc
Customer Loyalty scheme etc
Leading: Pricing business rules evaluated/prioritzed across more dynamic price options at the right time for the purchase transaction. Different product assortments may apply different dynamic pricing rule priorization at the time of purchase transaction.

Question_Text: Plan and Manage Promotional Items / Offers, involving modeling of promotional offets (prices, bundles etc.) to predict impact on sales to support the promotions planning process

Question_Text: Measure Promotional Effectiveness, tracking and assessing the impact of a promotion on sales of the promoted product, categories, affinity products and customer behaviour

Leading: Optimize promo space to maximize traffic and volume, by location. Track performance of promoted items in near real time. Change promotion or promotional pricing for different day parts. Store clustering based on shopping behavior  to drive cluster specific product placement.

Linking Customer movements to baskets to determine optimum layouts to drive larger baskets. Using Customer product affinities to select online product placement and co-location.
